title: Students head for country as AI bites
full_text:
Before Annalise Magill began her studies, she had been on a farm only on holidays.
"I had no real experience in agriculture before I chose my degree. I'd been on a farm in a very light capacity where I'd gone and had to look at some cows and some sheep, very much the city kid out of her depth," Magill, 19, said with a laugh.
As AI begins to eliminate entry-level roles and reshape the early-career landscape, Magill is among a cohort of young Australians who are turning towards a career in the $101 billion agriculture sector.
The Concord High School graduate is working as a junior agriculture economist at consultancy AgEcon while she studies for a bachelor of agricultural science at the University of Sydney.
"AI is not something I had considered when I applied for my degree, but it's definitely something that everyone is thinking about now. Agriculture jobs will never be replaced by AI - it might be able to do a monitoring map of your paddock, but it's probably not going to sit in the tractor for you.
"I'm not having that same level of anxiety and stress about my future in an industry because I don't feel as though it will be replaced by it," Magill said.
Agriculture remains short of workers - the Australian Farm Institute says there are six jobs for every agriculture graduate.
But remote work and the increased professionalisation of the sector (due to the internet) have done a lot to increase its appeal.
The end of the Millennium Drought and increased community understanding of supply chains thanks to panic buying during the pandemic have also helped to overcome its image problems of the past 40 years, says a 2021 paper published in International Journal of Innovation in Science and Mathematics Education.
Sharon Starick, a grain and pork producer from South Australia who is chair of the Council of Rural Research and Development Corporations, agrees.
Starick grew up on a wine-growing property in the Barossa and studied agricultural science "at a time when it was seen as an industry that wasn't going places, wasn't exciting" as producers suffered through drought and low commodity prices in the 1990s.
"There have been significant changes in farming, but also to the value chain, with new technology and new innovation. It's creating new jobs that are highly skilled and highly technical," she said.
Agriculture offered a range of roles, from working on a farm to communications, management, finance, policy, technology and research. "We need people from a diverse range of backgrounds, ages, genders, cultures. It brings diversity of thought to the way to approach the big challenges."
